name: Release Plan
purpose: A high-level schedule, similar to a roadmap, showing which release each requirement or user story is assigned to. What a release holds can change with the relative priority of the backlog items and the availability of the resources needed. It can be elaborated into sprints.

receives_from.what: the user stories or requirements assigned to releases come from the backlog (Table 6.3)
a high-level release plan may be developed after the product vision and backlog are started (prose); which fields flow is not stated in the book

alignment.what_must_agree: the releases must deliver what the vision promises (reading; the book gives only the list entry)
the book says 'Roadmap'; taken to be the project roadmap form; release timing must agree with it (reading; the book gives only the list entry)
the stories in each release must be the same items, in the same priority, as the backlog (reading; the book gives only the list entry)

elements.guidance: Either a timeline or a milestone marker for when releases start and finish; it can be more detailed, as a linear schedule showing each release's duration. The blank form prints no release date field, only the sprint columns.
The requirements or user stories taken from the backlog. The blank form shows them as sticky notes labelled User Story in the Sprint 1 to Sprint 4 columns and Team 1 to Team 4 lanes.

tailoring: As the plan gets more concrete, assign requirements or user stories to specific sprints in the release.
Arrange the plan in swim lanes, each lane assigned to a team or work stream.
Show the plan with a timeline to show relationships between user stories or features; this blends release content with schedule information.
agile_or_adaptive: The book places this form in its Agile chapter and says the agile forms can be tailored for any project regardless of development method. The prose says a release can be elaborated into several sprints, that once a sprint starts its requirements or user stories cannot be changed, and that the sequence and priorities may be updated after each sprint. The introduction suggests the Plan Schedule Management process: the release plan is a high-level schedule that may take the place of a schedule management plan, or serve as a high-level schedule for agile teams on small projects (Agile chapter introduction, PDF page 250, printed page 239).

decisions.decision: Which release each requirement or user story goes into
decisions.recorded_in: User Story notes under Sprint columns
decisions.notes: Updated by relative priority in the backlog and by the availability of resources, per the prose; the book states no further rule.

decisions.decision: When each release starts and finishes
decisions.notes: Table 6.3 names release dates, but the blank form prints no field for them.

decisions.decision: Whether and when stories are assigned to specific sprints
decisions.notes: Once a sprint starts its stories cannot be changed (prose).

decisions.decision: What the release is meant to achieve
decisions.notes: Printed on the blank form only.

citation: Book of Forms form 6.3, PDF page 255 (printed page 244); Table 6.3 PDF page 255 (printed page 244); blank form PDF page 256 (printed page 245); Agile chapter introduction PDF page 250 (printed page 239)
notes: pmbok_processes is empty because the Agile chapter introduction says PMBOK 6 lists none of the agile forms as an output of any process; it suggests Plan Schedule Management as the process where the release plan is most useful. The prose has no receives-from or provides-to section; the 6.2 entry comes from Table 6.3 and the 6.1 entry from the prose. provides_to is empty because no recipient is stated. The blank form's title block prints Project Name, not Project Title, and has no Date Prepared; it also prints a Release Goal row, which Table 6.3 does not list. Both printed_label values are empty because the blank form prints neither element name as a label. 'Roadmap' in the Alignment list is not a form name; reading it as 2.3 is an assumption.
